title: William Twisse distinguishes concurrence from predetermination and rejects the Jesuits' indifferent concurrence
source_text: XLIV. Tuissus autem Theologus Anglus distinguit concursum Dei ab ejus praedeterminatione, licet utrumque necessarium putet ad omnes creaturae actiones. Et concursum quidem agnoscit esse simul & natura, & tempore cum operatione creaturae, sed vult ipsi adjunctam esse motionem quandam praeviam in ipsam voluntatem. Etiam concursum, inquit, admittimus simultaneum tam natura quam tempore in actum; sed concursum istum dicimus complicare motionem praeviam in ipsam Voluntatem, praeviam, inquam, non tempore, sed natura. Vindiciarum lib. 2. part. 3. Et in eodem lib. pag. 18. Concursum indifferentem & indeterminatum, qualem Jesuitae docent, his Verbis respuit, Ego vero concursum istum indifferentem atque indefinitum perperam institui tam evidenter demonstrari posse existimo, quam solem meridianum lucere.
pass_a_gloss: But Twisse an English Theologian distinguishes the concurrence of God from his predetermination, although he thinks both necessary for all actions of the creature. And the concurrence indeed he acknowledges to be together both in nature, and in time with the operation of the creature, but will have joined to it a certain previous motion into the will itself. We also admit, he says, a concurrence simultaneous as well in nature as in time into the act; but that concurrence we say to involve a previous motion into the Will itself, previous, I say, not in time, but in nature. Of the Vindiciae book 2. part 3. And in the same book page 18. He rejects a Concurrence indifferent and undetermined, such as the Jesuits teach, in these Words, But I think that that indifferent and indefinite concurrence can be demonstrated to be wrongly devised as evidently as that the midday sun shines.
pass_b_english: The English theologian William Twisse distinguishes God's concurrence from his predetermination, though he thinks both necessary for every action of the creature. He grants that the concurrence is simultaneous with the creature's operation in both nature and time, but he insists that it is joined with a certain prior motion on the will itself.

'We too admit a concurrence on the act,' he says, 'simultaneous both in nature and in time; but we say that this concurrence involves a prior motion on the will itself, prior, I mean, not in time but in nature' (Vindiciae, book 2, part 3). In the same book, at page 18, he rejects an indifferent and undetermined concurrence of the kind the Jesuits teach: 'For my part I think it can be shown that this indifferent and indefinite concurrence is wrongly posited, as plainly as that the sun shines at noon.'

lemmas.latin: praeviam, inquam, non tempore, sed natura
lemmas.gloss: previous, I say, not in time, but in nature

choices.why: The Schools' term for God's acting together with secondary causes; 'concurrence' keeps it recognizable as the technical term, with 'cooperation' kept for cooperatio.
